description: Compare two fictional eight-fixture lighting scopes, identify exclusions and unresolved access, and download a blank proposal comparison record.
articleHtml:
JournalCost & planning/Cost and project scope

Price the same brief before comparing the totals

Reviewed November 22, 2026 · Lumascapes

A fixture count leaves several questions unanswered: which parts of the property are included, how the proposed equipment will be reached and connected, what is excluded, and who returns to review the scene after dark. Write down those differences before asking why two proposals have different totals.

This guide is a scope-planning exercise. It does not publish Lumascapes prices or estimate an installation from a photograph. Use the installation cost guide for the broader discussion and the quote checklist when reviewing a written proposal.

A fictional eight-fixture comparison

Suppose a homeowner wants an entry route, a patio, and two trees considered. The two fictional concepts below each list eight fixtures. The quantities are invented to illustrate a scope difference; neither concept is a design recommendation, an actual quote, or a completed project.

Equal counts, different coverage
Area in the homeowner briefConcept AConcept BQuestion before pricing
Entry route6 fixtures4 fixturesWhat route and transitions does each layout address?
Two trees2 fixtures2 fixturesAre the intended views and equipment the same?
Patio0 fixtures; omitted2 fixtures; includedDoes the brief require a separate patio scene?
Total8 fixtures8 fixturesEqual totals do not establish equivalent work.

Concept A leaves the patio out. Concept B allocates fewer fixtures to the entry. Neither count tells you whether a route is adequately lit, whether an exposed light source is uncomfortable, or whether the equipment and controls are equivalent. Ask for the intended result and inclusions to be described; do not divide the total by eight and treat that as a comparable unit price.

Download the fictional quantities (CSV). Both concept totals reconcile to eight. No prices, measured illumination, or customer observations are included.

Resolve six scope differences

  1. Coverage: mark each entry, path, gathering area, and feature included. Identify requested areas left out.
  2. Equipment: ask for the proposed fixture, light-source, transformer, and control details. A shared fixture count does not establish matching equipment.
  3. Route and access: identify paved crossings, planting beds, walls, and areas the installer has not inspected. Ask who confirms a workable route; do not assume a line on a sketch establishes access.
  4. Existing system: record equipment proposed for reuse and who assesses compatibility and condition. Keep unverified reuse as an open question.
  5. Finishing and follow-up: clarify surface restoration, debris removal, nighttime aiming, and what any return visit includes. Separate these from ongoing maintenance.
  6. Changes and exclusions: ask what happens if a concealed condition changes the scope, how additional work is approved, and which items remain outside the quoted total.

Use an uncertainty list rather than an assumed allowance

For example, if the route across a patio has not been reviewed, write “crossing method and restoration responsibility unconfirmed.” Ask the installer to explain how that uncertainty is addressed in the proposal. Do not enter zero simply because a separate line item is absent, or assume that one quote includes the same work as another.

Download a blank scope comparison record (CSV). Record each proposal's wording, the open question, the person confirming it, and the dated answer. Keep the original proposal with the record.

Discuss the lighting result as well as the installation

The DarkSky and Illuminating Engineering Society principles emphasize a defined purpose, directing light where needed, restrained output, appropriate controls, and warmer light where possible. Ask how the proposed scenes address those aims. These principles do not supply a fixture count, price, or local approval for your property.

If work must be staged, use the whole-property phasing example to separate the first phase from later work. Discuss the complete brief with Lumascapes installation services or start a project conversation.

description: Plan a sloped-yard lighting consultation with three fictional viewpoints, an observation checklist and a blank record for upper, lower and indoor views.
articleHtml:
JournalCost & planning/Pittsburgh property guide

Record the view from each level of the yard

Reviewed November 22, 2026 · Lumascapes

A hillside brief should describe more than the view from the upper deck. Include the lower approach, the transitions between levels, and the view from inside. These are separate observation points: a concept that looks appealing from one point still needs to be reviewed from the others.

This is a homeowner observation and consultation worksheet, not a fixture-placement plan. Use existing accessible routes in conditions you can navigate comfortably. Record an inaccessible area as “not observed” and arrange an on-site review; the worksheet does not call for climbing a slope, entering a neighbor's property, or moving electrical equipment.

A fictional three-viewpoint brief

Imagine an upper deck, steps to a lower gate, and a room facing the yard. This is an invented planning example, not a Lumascapes installation. There are no measured light levels or observed results. Before a demonstration, all comfort and visibility findings remain untested.

Three observations to request for the same concept
ViewpointPurpose in this fictional briefCheck during an agreed demonstrationCurrent finding
V1 — upper deck, standingSee the route toward the lower gateCan the route and level changes be distinguished without an uncomfortable exposed source?Untested
V2 — lower gate, facing uphillApproach the steps and upper landingWhat is visible when looking toward the higher level? Does a source face this viewpoint?Untested
V3 — inside room, seatedEnjoy the yard through the windowHow do the yard, reflections, and visible light sources appear with normal indoor lights on?Untested

Give every photograph a viewpoint label

Make a simple sketch linking V1, V2, and V3 to the property. Record the direction you face, whether you are standing or seated, the date, weather, existing lights in use, and the photograph filename. A daytime photo can show the route and planting; an evening photo records a different condition. Keep both labels rather than treating them as interchangeable evidence.

Phone exposure can change how bright a scene appears. Use photos to locate concerns and explain the brief, not as a substitute for agreed on-site observations or required measurements. The nighttime walkthrough guide helps organize the review.

Separate a concern from a tested finding

  • Concern: “A light above the lower gate may be visible from below.” This is a question to test, not a recorded glare failure.
  • Observed finding: record the viewpoint, conditions, and what the person actually saw during the demonstration. Avoid substituting a daytime drawing for that observation.
  • Follow-up: identify the change to review, who will review it, and the unresolved point. Retest the affected viewpoints rather than closing an issue because one view improved.

Download the blank viewpoint record (CSV). Leave unknown conditions marked unknown. The blank file contains no customer information or prefilled passing results.

Put site constraints on the same sketch

Mark walls, existing steps, planting, accessible routes, and equipment you know about; distinguish confirmed features from assumed routes. Ask the installer to assess access and the proposed connection route. Discuss planned planting or construction that could change the view. A lighting observation does not establish that a retaining wall, stair, or electrical installation is compliant or sound.

For discussion of light direction, shielding, output, and controls, see the DarkSky/IES responsible-lighting principles. Use them to frame questions about where light is needed and where it should be limited; they do not certify this fictional concept or replace site-specific requirements.

Bring a short, usable brief

Send the labeled sketch, a few relevant photos, the routes and views you care about, and the unanswered questions. Review path and step lighting, deck lighting, and the scope comparison example when discussing priorities. Contact Lumascapes to confirm an appropriate review for the property.
